title: The Part of Jeremiah 29:11 Most People Skip
paragraphs:
The Part of Jeremiah 29:11 Most People Skip
What God Said Before the Promise… and Why It Changes Everything

You’ve probably heard it quoted in moments that needed comfort. Maybe someone sent it to you when your life felt like it was falling apart, when doors closed, when prayers seemed to echo back unanswered.
“For I know the plans I have for you…”
It sounds like relief. It sounds like rescue. It sounds like God stepping in just in time.
But what if I told you that most people are holding onto the ending of that verse while completely ignoring the beginning of the story… the part that actually gives it weight?
Because Jeremiah 29:11 wasn’t written to people standing in victory.
It was written to people sitting in exile.
And if you miss that, you miss everything.

The original Hebrew carries a depth that English barely touches. When God says, “For I know the plans I have for you,” the word used is “מַחֲשָׁבוֹת” (machashavot), not casual thoughts, but intentional, deeply formed purposes—strategic, deliberate designs that are already in motion.
God isn’t guessing your future.
He already authored it.
But here’s the part that most people skip.
The verse right before.
Jeremiah 29:10:
“כִּי כֹה אָמַר יְהוָה… כִּי לְפִי מְלֹאת לְבָבֶל שִׁבְעִים שָׁנָה אֶפְקֹד אֶתְכֶם…”
“For thus says the LORD… when seventy years are completed for Babylon, I will visit you…”
Seventy years.
Not seventy minutes. Not seventy days. Not even a short season.
Seventy years of waiting.
Seventy years of being in a place they didn’t choose.
Seventy years of praying and not seeing immediate change.
Seventy years of feeling like God’s promise was delayed.
And then… after that… comes the verse we love to quote.
“For I know the plans…”
Let that sit with you.
Because suddenly, this verse isn’t a quick escape.
It’s a covenant spoken into captivity.
It’s God saying, “Even here… especially here… I am still writing your story.”
Some of you are in that kind of place right now.
Not the Instagram version of struggle.
Not the kind you can fix with motivation.
The kind where you wake up and still feel stuck.
The kind where you pray but heaven feels silent.
The kind where your reality doesn’t match the promise you’ve been holding onto.
And if you’re honest, there are moments where you wonder if God forgot you.
But the Hebrew doesn’t allow that interpretation.
Because God didn’t say, “I will come up with plans.”
He said, “I KNOW the plans.”
Already written.
Already secured.
Already moving behind what you can see.
And when He says those plans are for “peace,” the word is “שָׁלוֹם” (shalom).
Not just peace as in calm feelings.
Shalom means wholeness. Completion. Restoration. Nothing missing, nothing broken.
God isn’t promising you comfort.
He’s promising to make you whole again.
Even if the process feels like exile.
Even if the timeline stretches longer than you expected.
Even if you don’t recognize yourself in the middle of it.
Because the truth is… the exile was never the end of their story.
It was the place where God stripped away idols, rebuilt identity, and prepared a people who would finally understand dependence on Him.
And maybe that’s why this hits harder than we expected.
Because we love the promise…
But we resist the process that makes the promise meaningful.
You want Jeremiah 29:11 to be real in your life?
Then you have to accept Jeremiah 29:10 too.
The waiting.
The refining.
The seasons that don’t make sense yet.
That doesn’t mean God has abandoned you.
It means He’s still writing.
And when the New Testament echoes this truth, it goes even deeper.
In Romans 8:28, the Greek says:
“πάντα συνεργεῖ εἰς ἀγαθόν…”
“All things work together for good…”
“Synergei”—to work together, to cooperate, to weave into a greater outcome.
Even the exile.
Even the pain.
Even the silence.
Even the parts of your story you wish you could erase.
God is weaving it.
Not wasting it.
And that’s where Jesus steps into the story and changes everything.
Because the ultimate “exile” wasn’t Babylon.
It was separation from God.
And Christ didn’t just speak promises into that condition…
He entered it.
He carried it.
He redeemed it.
The Gospel isn’t God saying, “Hold on, it’ll get better.”
It’s God saying, “I came to get you, even in the middle of it.”
So when you read Jeremiah 29:11 again, don’t read it like a motivational quote.
Read it like a letter written to people who thought their story was over.
Read it like a whisper from God into your darkest moment.
“I still know the plans…”
Be honest.
Someone else needs to see that they’re not alone in this.
And if you’ve been fed, challenged, or awakened by this, don’t stay distant from the source.
Because this was never just about one verse.
It’s about a God who speaks purpose into pain… and then walks with you through it until the promise becomes reality.
He didn’t skip your story.
Don’t skip His process.
